analysis.one_liner: Removes states' ability to opt out of the federal private school scholarship tax credit.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on September 16, 2026, and has seen no further action; it has two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law created a tax credit for people who donate to scholarship organizations that pay private school tuition for elementary and secondary students, but only in states that choose to participate. This bill would delete that state opt-in, so the credit would operate in all fifty states, including the ones that declined. States that said no would have the federal private-school subsidy imposed on them anyway.
analysis.who_benefits: Private schools and scholarship-granting organizations gain a nationwide pipeline of federal tax-credit-funded tuition. Donors who claim the credit, and families who receive the scholarships, also gain, with the donor benefit rising with the ability to give.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Private schools, scholarship groups, and donor households

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates the state opt-in requirement for the qualified elementary and secondary education scholarship credit, making the credit available nationwide rather than only in participating states.

Under the credit, donations to scholarship-granting organizations that fund K-12 private school tuition earn a federal tax credit; the bill would let that channel operate even in states that chose not to take part.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost of the credits claimed. Residents of states that opted out have their state's decision overridden, and public school systems in those states could lose students and the per-pupil funding that follows them as the subsidized private-school channel operates anyway.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, opt-out states, and public schools

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides the choice of states that decided not to participate in the scholarship credit, replacing a state-decision structure with a federally imposed one.

The credit subsidizes private school tuition through donors; as more students use it, public schools can lose enrollment and the per-pupil funding attached to it, with no offsetting funding in the bill.
The benefit is a tax credit for people who donate, so the direct advantage goes to households with the income and tax liability to give, rather than being distributed per child.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does help some families afford private school by expanding the scholarship channel nationwide. The cost is federal revenue forgone and the removal of the state opt-in that let states decline the program; the strongest objection is not the scholarships themselves but imposing the subsidy on states that explicitly said no, while public schools in those states face enrollment-driven funding pressure without any compensating support.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in mid-September 2026 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it with the session ending January 3, 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Adrian Smith introduced the bill on September 16, 2026, to eliminate the state opt-in requirement for the qualified elementary and secondary education scholarship credit.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day and has had no further action.
Two House Republicans have cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: taxpayers and public schools are unaffected, and states that opted out of the scholarship credit still keep their choice. The private-school tax credit remains limited to participating states.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opt-out states, so far, keep their choice

for.name: Rep. Adrian Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 16, 2026, to eliminate the state opt-in requirement for the scholarship credit.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action since the bill was referred on September 16, 2026; no markup, no vote, no floor referral.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Republicans appear on the bill (the sponsor plus two cosponsors), no Democrat has cosponsored it, and no vote has occurred, so no real partisan pattern has formed.

industries.industry: Private K-12 schools and scholarship-granting organizations
industries.note: The bill makes the federal donation tax credit available in every state, turning the scholarship organizations into a permanent, nationwide channel for taxpayer-subsidized private tuition. It matters because it would route that subsidy even into states whose governments chose not to participate.

A subsidized private-school channel operating in opt-out states can draw students away, and public school funding generally follows enrollment. The bill provides no offsetting support to the schools losing those students.
The credit rewards making donations, so the direct tax benefit scales with the ability to give. Expanding it nationwide increases the total federal revenue forgone to donors.

analysis.trajectory: With only two cosponsors, a referral to Ways and Means in mid-September 2026, and no committee action before the session ends January 3, 2027, the bill is almost certain to die in committee without a vote.
